Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Redis Pub/Sub Messaging

Redis Pub/Sub Messaging

A fast, ephemeral broadcast system: publishers tag messages by channel, and currently connected subscribers receive those messages instantly. This slide deck teaches commands, patterns, uses, and limitations.

In this lesson

Understand PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, and the fire-and-forget delivery model. Run the provided redis-cli examples yourself in three terminals to see live behavior.

Why it matters

Pub/Sub enables chat, live dashboards, and notifications with minimal latency and low operational complexity. But it trades persistence for speed.

screens.narratorSegment: These second set of objectives guides practical activity and decision-making. Hands-on

Three-session terminal demo

Why this matters

Actual terminals reveal how SUBSCRIBE locks a connection for receiving messages and how PSUBSCRIBE matches many channels at once.

Design decisions

screens.title: Pub/Sub pattern explained
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: Publish/Subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders publish messages to named channels and receivers subscribe to channels they care about. Publishers do not target individual receivers; instead, they categorize messages by channel name. This decoupling matters because it reduces tight coupling between services: a producer of events does not need to know who consumes them. As a concrete example, think of a sports news feed: the scoreboard service publishes updates to channels like news:sports or game:football:123. Any client that has subscribed to those channels receives updates while it is connected. A common misconception is to assume Pub/Sub buffers or stores messages for later subscribers. It does not. If no clients are subscribed at publish time, the message is discarded. That trade-off explains why Pub/Sub is extremely fast but not suitable for guaranteed delivery or replay. Key takeaway: use Pub/Sub for immediate, ephemeral broadcasts where latency is critical but persistence is not. Pub/Sub pattern explained means publishers send to channels, subscribers listen; decoupling makes real-time systems simpler but ephemeral.. In practical terms, decoupling senders and receivers with channels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Pub/Sub pattern explained
Definition

Publish/Subscribe in one sentence

A publisher sends messages to named channels; subscribers listen to channels and receive messages while connected.

Analogy

Think of a bulletin board with labeled sections. Anyone can post to a section; anyone currently watching that section sees new posts immediately.

Common misconception

Do not assume messages are queued for later viewers. Pub/Sub is ephemeral; it does not store messages for disconnected subscribers.

Key Takeaway

Pub/Sub decouples producers and consumers for low-latency broadcasts but sacrifices persistence and delivery guarantees.

Concrete example
A live sports feed publishes score updates to game-specific channels. Fans subscribed to those channels see updates instantly while connected.
# In redis-cli (publisher)
PUBLISH news:sports "Local team wins championship!"

# Any clients subscribed to news:sports will receive the message immediately.

screens.title: Core commands: PUBLISH
screens.narratorSegment: The PUBLISH command is the publisher's primary tool. You issue a PUBLISH with a channel name and message content and Redis delivers that payload to all currently subscribed clients for that channel. For example, a notification service might publish a short JSON payload or plain text alert to a channel like app:updates:critical. The act of publishing is synchronous from the client perspective: Redis returns the number of clients that received the message, but it does not persist the message for future subscribers. A concrete example is running a publisher in a redis-cli session and observing the integer reply showing how many subscribers were online. A common misunderstanding is to equate that integer with a delivery guarantee; it only shows how many clients were active at the time, not whether they processed the message. The practical takeaway is to keep messages small for low bandwidth usage and to design for possible message loss if subscribers disconnect. If you need replay or durability, choose Redis Streams or a different queuing system. Core commands: PUBLISH means publish sends a message and returns the count of current recipients; messages are not stored for later delivery.. In practical terms, how publishers send messages to channels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › PUBLISH
Command

PUBLISH channel message

Send a message to a named channel. Redis returns how many clients were delivered the message, not whether it was persisted.

# In redis-cli (publisher)
PUBLISH news:sports "Local team wins championship!"

# Redis returns an integer reply showing how many subscribers received it.
Practical tip

Keep messages small to reduce bandwidth when publishing to many subscribers. The server sends the message to every subscriber, so size matters.

Misconception

The integer reply is not an acknowledgement of processing — only an indication of how many clients were connected at publish time.

Scenario

A monitoring service publishes critical alerts to app:updates:critical. Connected dashboards receive alerts in real time. If a dashboard is offline when the alert is published, it will miss that alert.

Key Takeaway

PUBLISH is immediate and ephemeral. Use it when speed matters and you accept possible loss for offline subscribers.

screens.title: SUBSCRIBE and subscriber behavior
screens.narratorSegment: SUBSCRIBE is how clients express interest in one or more channels. When a client issues SUBSCRIBE, that connection enters a receive-only mode: Redis dedicates the socket to delivering messages and will not accept arbitrary commands on that connection until the client unsubscribes. Practically, this means many client libraries create a separate connection for subscriptions while using another for normal Redis commands. A concrete example is starting a redis-cli session, running SUBSCRIBE news:sports, and watching incoming messages appear as they are published. A frequent mistake is trying to issue standard read or write commands on a subscription connection; those commands will be ignored because the connection is in subscription mode. Another important detail is message format: Redis pushes the message type, the channel name, and the message content in a structured reply. Key takeaway: use separate connections if your application both subscribes and needs to perform other Redis operations, and plan your client architecture accordingly. SUBSCRIBE and subscriber behavior means subscribe locks a connection into receive-only mode; use separate connections for other redis operations.. In practical terms, how subscribers receive messages and dedicated connection mode. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › SUBSCRIBE
How it works

SUBSCRIBE locks the connection

Once subscribed, the connection becomes dedicated to receiving delivered messages and does not accept normal Redis commands until unsubscribed.

# Subscriber session
SUBSCRIBE news:sports news:politics

# Messages will be pushed to this connection as they arrive.
Design note

Give subscription tasks their own client connections if the application also needs to query or update Redis data structures.

Message format

A delivered message includes a message type identifier, the channel name, and the message payload. Clients receive these structured replies and parse them according to their libraries.

Misconception

Trying to use a subscription connection for unrelated commands will not work; the client must unsubscribe first or use another connection.

Key Takeaway

Use separate connections for subscribing and for normal Redis operations to avoid locked connections and unexpected behavior.

screens.title: UNSUBSCRIBE and subscription lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: UNSUBSCRIBE lets a client stop listening on channels. You can specify individual channel names to stop or call UNSUBSCRIBE with no arguments to remove all current subscriptions on that connection. When a client unsubscribes from every channel, the connection exits subscription mode and returns to a normal command-capable state. A useful scenario is a client that temporarily listens to a feed and then needs to perform writes; it should call UNSUBSCRIBE or use a second connection. A common error is forgetting to unsubscribe before closing a connection, which may leave assumptions about client state on the application side. In many deployment patterns, subscription clients are long-lived and handle reconnection logic to maintain live updates. Key takeaway: manage subscription lifecycle explicitly and design reconnection strategies so clients can re-subscribe after network interruptions. UNSUBSCRIBE and subscription lifecycle means use unsubscribe to leave channels; when no subscriptions remain, the connection returns to normal command mode.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › UNSUBSCRIBE
Command

UNSUBSCRIBE [channel ...]

Stop receiving messages from specified channels or from all channels if no arguments are provided. When no subscriptions remain, the connection exits subscription mode.

# Stop listening to a channel
UNSUBSCRIBE news:sports

# Stop all subscriptions
UNSUBSCRIBE
Lifecycle notes
  • Unsubscribe explicitly when a client needs to repurpose its connection for other commands.
  • Handle reconnection and re-subscription in client code to survive network interruptions.
  • Avoid leaving many transient subscription connections open without cleanup.
Key Takeaway

Manage subscriptions intentionally. Use UNSUBSCRIBE and reconnection logic so subscription clients remain healthy and predictable.

screens.title: Pattern subscriptions with PSUBSCRIBE
screens.narratorSegment: PSUBSCRIBE allows clients to subscribe to channel name patterns using glob-style wildcards. The most common wildcard is the asterisk, which matches any sequence of characters, so subscribing to news:* captures news:sports, news:politics, and other channels that start with news:. Pattern subscriptions are powerful when your system organizes channels hierarchically and you want a single listener to receive related events. For example, an admin dashboard might PSUBSCRIBE app:updates:* to receive critical, info, and debug updates across the application. When Redis delivers a pattern-matched message, it uses a distinct message type indicating the matched pattern and the actual channel that generated the message, so subscribers can inspect both. A common error is overbroad patterns that unintentionally match many channels, increasing bandwidth and processing load. Key takeaway: use PSUBSCRIBE for flexible grouping, but design patterns to avoid excessive fan-out and unintentional matches. Pattern subscriptions with PSUBSCRIBE means psubscribe matches channel name patterns and sends messages with information about the pattern and actual channel; use judiciously to limit fan-out.. In practical terms, using wildcards to subscribe to multiple channels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › PSUBSCRIBE
Pattern matching

PSUBSCRIBE news:*

Use glob wildcards to subscribe to groups of channels. The asterisk matches any sequence, and the question mark matches a single character.

# Pattern subscriber
PSUBSCRIBE news:*

# This will receive messages published to news:sports and news:politics, etc.
Practical tip

Design channel naming carefully so patterns match the intended set without accidental overlap with other domains.

Warning

An overly broad pattern can increase bandwidth and CPU usage on subscribers. Audit patterns in production to avoid surprises.

Message metadata

When Redis pushes a pattern-matched message, it includes the pattern and the originating channel name, enabling the subscriber to route or filter further if needed.

Key Takeaway

PSUBSCRIBE simplifies subscribing to hierarchical channels, but use precise patterns to avoid unintended fan-out.

screens.title: Fire-and-forget semantics
screens.narratorSegment: A central characteristic of Redis Pub/Sub is its fire-and-forget delivery model. In plain terms, Redis sends published messages to subscribers that are currently connected, and it does not retain or re-deliver messages to clients that connect later. This design favors low latency and minimal server-side overhead. Consider a live chat: when a user publishes a message to chat:room:42, only users currently connected and subscribed to that channel will see it. If a user reconnects later, they will not receive messages sent while they were offline. Compare this to message queues or Redis Streams which persist messages and support replay or acknowledgement semantics. A typical misconception is to treat Pub/Sub like a durable queue. The practical impact is significant: for critical events that must be processed exactly once, Pub/Sub alone is insufficient. The takeaway is to use Pub/Sub for ephemeral, real-time updates and to pair it with persistent structures if you require durability, replay, or consumer acknowledgement. Fire-and-forget semantics means pub/sub delivers only to connected subscribers at publish time. no persistence, no replay, no acknowledgements.. In practical terms, why pub/sub does not guarantee delivery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ephemeral vs persistent

Pub/Sub is ephemeral by design

Messages are delivered only to currently connected subscribers. If nobody is listening the message is discarded.

Contrast

Compare Pub/Sub to Redis Streams or queues which persist messages and enable replay and acknowledgement semantics.

Misconception

Do not rely on Pub/Sub for durable delivery or exactly-once processing. It is not a replacement for persistent messaging systems.

A scoreboard publishes play-by-play updates. Fans who disconnect and reconnect will not receive missed plays. If replay is required, buffer events in a persistent store or use Streams.

Fire-and-forget gives speed. If durability or replay are requirements, choose a persistent model instead of plain Pub/Sub.

screens.title: Scaling, volume, and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Designing Pub/Sub at scale requires thinking about fan-out and connection patterns. When a message is published to a channel with many subscribers, Redis delivers the message individually to each subscriber, so network bandwidth and server C P U can become bottlenecks. Keep messages compact and consider sharding channels or filtering subscriptions to reduce unnecessary traffic. Also plan your client connection strategy: subscription connections are long-lived, and libraries often provide reconnection logic. If your application needs to both subscribe and perform other Redis operations, use separate connections for each role to avoid blocked command attempts. A common operational mistake is creating many short-lived subscription connections, which increases overhead and complicates resource usage. Key takeaway: estimate subscriber counts and message sizes, choose channel schemes that limit fan-out, and use separate connections and reconnection policies for robust behavior under real traffic. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Scaling & Safety
Fan-out costs

Each published message is delivered to every subscriber. Multiply message size by subscriber count to estimate bandwidth and server load.

Practical steps
  • Use narrow channels for selective subscriptions.
  • Keep payloads small and encode efficiently.
  • Shard topics when subscriber counts grow very large.
Connection hygiene

Avoid many short-lived subscription connections. Prefer long-lived clients with robust reconnection and re-subscription handling.

When to choose alternatives

If you need guaranteed delivery, replay, or consumer groups, choose Redis Streams or a dedicated messaging system instead of Pub/Sub.

Checklist

Estimate fan-out, plan for small messages, use separate connections, and pick Streams for durability.

Today we will explore Redis Pub/Sub, a lightweight messaging pattern built into Redis for real-time broadcasts. You will learn the core commands used to send and receive messages, how pattern subscriptions make channel hierarchies flexible, and why Pub/Sub is described as “fire-and-forget.” Imagine a chat room or live scoreboard: publishers place messages on named channels, and any clients currently listening on those channels receive them instantly. That decouples senders and receivers so systems scale without tight coupling. We will walk through exact redis-cli examples you can run, show how pattern matching catches groups of channels, and surface common misconceptions—especially the expectation of persistence or guaranteed delivery. By the end, you will be able to design a simple notification flow, choose appropriate commands for publishers and subscribers, and know when Redis Pub/Sub is not the right tool because of its ephemeral delivery model. Consider a chat room where a late-arriving user expects prior messages; that expectation will drive a different design than Pub/Sub.

These learning objectives map to practical skills you will practice. First, you will explain the Publish/Subscribe pattern: what channels are, how publishers and subscribers interact, and why this decoupling matters for real-time systems. Second, you'll use the core Redis commands to send and receive messages — specifically the PUBLISH command to send a message and SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE to receive and stop receiving messages. Third, you'll implement pattern-based subscriptions with PSUBSCRIBE and PUNSUBSCRIBE so you can capture groups of channels with a single subscription. Fourth, you will identify real-world use cases such as chat rooms, live dashboards, and notification broadcasting and recognize how Pub/Sub simplifies these flows. Each objective pairs definition with short hands-on practice so you not only know the commands but also understand when to use them. As you work through examples, check the common misconception that Pub/Sub persists messages; it does not. Keep that contrast in mind as you learn.

These second set of objectives guides practical activity and decision-making. First, you will build and run a three-terminal exercise where one terminal publishes and two subscribe — one to a specific channel and one to a pattern. This hands-on practice makes the abstract commands concrete and reveals the dedicated-connection behavior of subscribers. Second, you will learn to distinguish Pub/Sub from persistent streams or queues. When you need message persistence, acknowledgements, or replay, Pub/Sub is not appropriate; Streams or a queueing system is a better choice. Third, you will evaluate scaling and safety concerns: how message fan-out behaves when many subscribers are attached and why message size and subscriber count affect resource planning. Fourth, you will be able to articulate the key limitation: no delivery guarantees for offline subscribers. These skills will help you pick Pub/Sub for low-latency, ephemeral broadcasts and avoid it when guaranteed delivery matters.

Start with a clear definition: Publish/Subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders publish messages to named channels and receivers subscribe to channels they care about. Publishers do not target individual receivers; instead, they categorize messages by channel name. This decoupling matters because it reduces tight coupling between services: a producer of events does not need to know who consumes them. As a concrete example, think of a sports news feed: the scoreboard service publishes updates to channels like news:sports or game:football:123. Any client that has subscribed to those channels receives updates while it is connected. A common misconception is to assume Pub/Sub buffers or stores messages for later subscribers. It does not. If no clients are subscribed at publish time, the message is discarded. That trade-off explains why Pub/Sub is extremely fast but not suitable for guaranteed delivery or replay. Key takeaway: use Pub/Sub for immediate, ephemeral broadcasts where latency is critical but persistence is not. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The PUBLISH command is the publisher's primary tool. You issue a PUBLISH with a channel name and message content and Redis delivers that payload to all currently subscribed clients for that channel. For example, a notification service might publish a short JSON payload or plain text alert to a channel like app:updates:critical. The act of publishing is synchronous from the client perspective: Redis returns the number of clients that received the message, but it does not persist the message for future subscribers. A concrete example is running a publisher in a redis-cli session and observing the integer reply showing how many subscribers were online. A common misunderstanding is to equate that integer with a delivery guarantee; it only shows how many clients were active at the time, not whether they processed the message. The practical takeaway is to keep messages small for low bandwidth usage and to design for possible message loss if subscribers disconnect. If you need replay or durability, choose Redis Streams or a different queuing system. SUBSCRIBE is how clients express interest in one or more channels. Let's summarize the key concepts you should remember. First, Publish/Subscribe is a decoupled messaging pattern where publishers send to channels and subscribers listen; it's excellent for low-latency broadcasts. Second, core commands include PUBLISH to send messages, SUBSCRIBE and UNSUBSCRIBE to start and stop listening, and PSUBSCRIBE and PUNSUBSCRIBE for pattern-based subscriptions. Third, Pub/Sub operates on a fire-and-forget model: messages are delivered only to currently connected subscribers and are not persisted for later consumption. Keep these three ideas in mind when designing real-time features, and pair Pub/Sub with persistent structures when durability or replay is required.
